newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries close lower after light session.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries close lower after light session.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices closed lower on Monday as the market remained nervous ahead of Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's testimony Wednesday.

Trade volume was light, with no new economic releases. Few market participants seemed to want to stake positions ahead of the central bank chief's comments. Also weighing on the market were a weak dollar and supply concerns, with the Treasury's regular weekly three- and six-month bills auctions Monday and the scheduled auction of two- and five-year notes on Tuesday and Wednesday, respectively.
The 30-year Treasury bond ended at 99-19/32, down 7/32 to yield 6.66 percent.

Adding to concern was the rescheduling of Greenspan's testimony before the House on Thursday to the following week on March 5 due to Chilean President Eduardo Frei's address to a joint session of Congress set for the same time.
"The market is just waiting for Greenspan to testify. Typically the markets are soft in front of the testimony," said William Dudley, senior economist at Goldman Sachs & Co.
Dudley expected Greenspan to pretty much say what he has been saying in recent public appearances.

"He's just going to say 'we think of a tightening as more likely but we have no idea when this will occur. The outlook is quite uncertain implying no change in monetary policy is imminent,'" Dudley said.

The bond market could rally based on such comments, but any relief rally probably wouldn't be very substantial, Dudley said. He saw no large problem with Greenspan's testimony being postponed as it should be essentially the same before the House as the Senate.
"Sometimes in Round Two the chairman decides to correct the markets reaction to his comments," Dudley allowed.

The market still had to absorb the February nonfarm payrolls report on March 7 and many forecasters expected the report to be quite strong. In addition, the National Association of Purchasing Management's survey was set for release on March 3.

"We did see some trading going on, but by and large it just looks like a lot of people were finishing off the squaring up that began a couple of weeks ago," said Christopher Low, senior economist at HSBC Markets Inc.
Most of the customers Monday were smaller players who typically square up later than large players, Low said.
Low expected Tuesday would be another day of light trading ahead of Greenspan's testimony.

"No one expects him to say anything surprising and anything surprising would probably be damaging. But assuming he doesn't, we'll probably see some large funds resuming to move further out on the curve" a process started several weeks ago, Low said.
The Treasury will sell $17.5 billion in two-year notes on Tuesday and $12.5 billion in five-year notes on Wednesday, making supply an issue at primary dealerships.
In when-issued trade on Monday, the two-year notes ended with a 5.87 percent yield. The five-year Treasury notes to be auctioned on Wednesday ended with a 6.175 percent yield.

At the short end of the maturity curve, three-month bill rates rose two basis points to 4.98 percent. Six-month bill rates were up one basis point at 5.03 percent and year-bill rates were up one basis point at 5.19 percent.

Two-year notes ended down 1/32 at 100-1/32, yielding 5.85 percent. Five-year notes closed at 100-10/32, down 1/32, yielding 6.17 percent. Ten-year notes ended at 99-even, down 4/32 to yield 6.39 percent.
